opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as complementary rather than competing. The way I'd put it is that the symbolic models, the kind of thing scientists have been building for centuries, differential equations, conservation laws, causal structure, have this enormous virtue: they're auditable. You can look at them, you can check them, you can reason about what they imply in regimes you haven't observed yet. And crucially, you can get guarantees out of them. If I have a model of how a power grid behaves, written down in a formal way, I can actually ask, "Is there any input sequence that leads to a blackout?" and get an answer I can trust, at least relative to the model.

What symbolic models are bad at is being written. It's extraordinarily labor-intensive for humans to build them, and they tend to be brittle at the edges, they leave out things that matter. Neural networks are almost the mirror image. They're incredibly good at soaking up messy, high-dimensional data and producing something that predicts well, but you can't really inspect them, and you certainly can't get a proof out of them about what will happen in a situation that's out of distribution.

So the vision I've been working toward is one where we use neural networks, and frontier AI systems in particular, as the engine that *generates* and *refines* symbolic world models, and then the symbolic models are the artifact we actually rely on for safety-critical reasoning. The AI does the creative, heuristic, intuition-heavy work of proposing structure, fitting parameters, finding where the model disagrees with data, and then that output gets checked, by formal verification tools and by comparison against reality, before we trust it. It's a bit like how we treat human scientists: we don't need to understand the neurons in Newton's head to trust the laws of motion, because the laws themselves are a checkable object.

And I'd add one nuance, which is that I don't think the right world model is purely symbolic in the old-fashioned sense. There's room for hybrid representations: probabilistic programs, models with explicit uncertainty, components that are learned but bounded in a way you can still reason about. The key property isn't "no neural networks anywhere," it's that the thing we're making decisions on is something whose behavior we can bound and verify. Neural nets are fantastic as the scientist; I'm just much more hesitant to have them be the science.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that these two things are actually complementary rather than competing, and the mistake that people have made for a long time is treating it as a dichotomy — either you're on the symbolic side or you're on the connectionist side.

If you look at how science actually works, we have this enormous accumulated body of symbolic models of the physical world. Differential equations, conservation laws, thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, chemistry — all of this is written down in formal mathematical language that humans have been refining for centuries. And the thing about those models is that they come with something neural networks don't have on their own, which is a story about why they're right and when they break down. A model of a bridge in a finite element solver isn't just a prediction; it's a prediction with a principled account of its own validity regime.

Neural networks, on the other hand, are extraordinarily good at something the symbolic tradition was always bad at, which is bridging the gap between messy, high-dimensional, unstructured observation and anything you could actually write an equation about. Vision, language, perception, pattern recognition — the things where nobody could ever write down the rules by hand.

So the vision I have is roughly this: you use neural networks as the interface. They're the thing that looks at the world, reads the literature, talks to the human, and proposes candidate models. But the actual reasoning about the physical world — the part where you want to be able to say "this intervention is safe," or "this system will stay within these bounds" — that should ultimately bottom out in symbolic, formally specified world models where you can check the reasoning rather than just trust it.

And the exciting part to me is that modern AI makes this tractable in a way it never was before. Historically the bottleneck for formal methods was that writing the specifications and the models was incredibly laborious — you needed a small army of PhDs to formalize even a modest system. Language models change that economics dramatically. You can have a system that reads a thousand papers on, say, battery chemistry, and produces a formal model, and then you can have another process that verifies that the model is consistent with the data and with the known physics.

I think of it as the neural network being the scientist's intuition and the symbolic model being the scientist's notebook. Intuition is where the ideas come from, but the notebook is what you actually trust, because it's what you can go back and audit. What we're trying to build is a pipeline where the intuition is machine intuition and the notebook is machine-checkable, and the critical thing is that the guarantees you care about live in the notebook, not in the intuition.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as complementary. A symbolic scientific model gives you an explicit account of the structure of a system: what the variables are, how they interact, and what assumptions you’re making. That’s useful because you can inspect those assumptions and reason about their consequences. But there’s a lot of work involved in connecting that model to the world—to noisy observations, images, or situations where you don’t already know which variables matter.

Neural networks can help with that connection. They can learn representations from observations, propose candidate models, and approximate computations that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. The distinction I’d make is between proposing something plausible and establishing that it follows from a set of assumptions. A network can be very good at the first without automatically giving you the second.

So the picture is a loop: use learning to identify structure and suggest hypotheses, use explicit models to derive predictions or check constraints, and then compare those predictions with observations. And you have to keep track of two different uncertainties: whether your reasoning is correct given the model, and whether the model adequately describes the physical system. Even a perfectly checked derivation doesn’t eliminate that second question.

r002.rationale: It says neural networks can approximate expensive computations, but does not state that a proof can certify a network has low approximation error.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss partial differential equations or explain that checking a candidate solution’s error can be easier than finding the solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as complementary. A symbolic scientific model gives you an explicit account of some aspect of the world: these are the variables, these are the relationships, and here are the assumptions under which those relationships hold. That’s very useful for reasoning, because you can inspect the model and ask what follows from it. But constructing the right model, and connecting its variables to messy observations, is itself a difficult problem.

Neural networks can help with that connection. They can learn representations from observations, suggest which quantities matter, and potentially propose models. You might have a network take in an image and infer a set of objects and their properties, and then use a physical model to reason about how those objects will move.

The interesting part is making that interaction go both ways. The model makes predictions, observations reveal where those predictions fail, and the learned system helps revise the model or recognize that you’re outside its domain of applicability. So the vision is a system that can move between learned representations and explicit models, while keeping track of what its conclusions actually depend on.
